# 2 Samuel 22:1–26 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Overview of the Chapter

This song (nearly identical to Psalm 18) is David's great retrospective psalm of praise, likely sung near the end of his life, looking back over decades of God's deliverances. John Piper calls it a "God-entranced, God-besotted song" — God is mentioned over 90 times in 51 verses. Constable divides the chapter into four sections: the Lord's exaltation (vv. 1–4), exploits (vv. 5–20), equity (vv. 21–30), and excellence (vv. 31–51). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-22.html; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/davids-god-entranced-song)

---

## v. 1 — And David sang this song to the LORD on the day the LORD had delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.

**Traditional reading:** Most commentators hold that this psalm was composed earlier in David's life (perhaps when Saul died and David first took the throne, 2 Sam 8:14) and then sung again in old age as a summary of God's lifelong faithfulness. Spurgeon suggests it was "sung by David at different times when he reviewed his own remarkable history." Matthew Henry notes that David "spoke…to the LORD, for his honour" — not just for personal pleasure or instruction but directly to God. Henry also observes the speed of David's thanksgiving: "in the day that God delivered him he sang this song. While the mercy is fresh…let the thank-offering be brought." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-samuel-22.html; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-22-commentary)

Saul is named separately, either because David refused to count him among "enemies" (since David did not hate Saul) or because Saul was the chief and most dangerous pursuer. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-samuel-22.html)

Piper adds that the relief was so striking that David called the cessation of hostilities "a day, as though it happened in a single day," and "virtually exploded with poetry and song." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/davids-god-entranced-song)

---

## v. 2 — He said: "The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer."

**Traditional reading:** Each title is drawn from David's experience. "Rock" (*sela'*) recalls the rocky crags and caves of the Judean wilderness where David hid from Saul, including the "Rock of Escape" (1 Sam 23:28). Spurgeon: "Dwelling among the crags and mountain fastnesses of Judea David had escaped the malice of Saul, and here he compares his God to such a place of concealment and security." The "fortress" (*mesudah*) recalls the strongholds where David took refuge (Adullam, 1 Sam 22:4). God as "Deliverer" (*palat*) means one who rescues, brings to safety, causes to escape. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-22-commentary)

The repeated possessive pronoun "my" (10 times in vv. 2–3) indicates not abstract theology but personal relationship. Precept Austin stresses this with Jesus' warning in Mt 7:21–23: "I never knew you." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-22-commentary)

**Reformed/Baptist (Piper):** The song begins by "exploding with ten names for God" — the focus from the very start is relentlessly on God, not David. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/davids-god-entranced-song)

---

## v. 3 — "My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation. My stronghold, my refuge, and my Savior, You save me from violence."

**Traditional reading:** The "horn of my salvation" is a symbol of strength and protection — the horn of an animal both defends and attacks. Matthew Henry: "by which I am strongly protected, and my enemies are strongly pushed." Henry also sees a Messianic link to Luke 1:69 where Christ is called the "horn of salvation." Guzik notes: "When we see God for who He is, it is easy to trust Him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-samuel-22.html)

---

## v. 4 — "I will call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised; so shall I be saved from my enemies."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon: "It is well to pray to God as to one who deserves to be praised, for then we plead in a happy and confident manner. If I feel that I can and do bless the Lord for all his past goodness, I am bold to ask great things of him." This verse is the thesis statement of the entire song — because God is worthy of praise, calling on Him brings salvation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-22-commentary)

---

## vv. 5–6 — "For the waves of death engulfed me; the torrents of chaos overwhelmed me. The cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me."

**Traditional reading:** David describes danger on every side — physically, spiritually, emotionally, socially. Matthew Henry: "He was surrounded with death on every side, threatened to be overwhelmed, and saw no way of escape." The imagery of waves, torrents, cords, and snares portrays death as an active, aggressive force. "The floods of Belial" (KJV: "ungodly men") made him afraid — not just abstract death but wicked men pursuing him. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-samuel-22.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/)

The Pulpit Commentary translates: "Breakers of death surrounded me, Streams of Belial terrified me, Cords of Sheol girt me about, Snares of death overtook me." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_samuel/22.htm)

---

## v. 7 — "In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God. And from His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for help reached His ears."

**Traditional reading:** David's prayer was simple, desperate, and effective. Guzik: "The enemy of our soul wants us to believe that we can't call upon the LORD in our distress — as if we had to be right with God and sitting peacefully in a prayer chapel to pray rightly. David knew that God hears our distress signals." Constable notes that "temple" here probably means heaven (God's heavenly dwelling), not the earthly temple (which wasn't built yet). Ellicott notes that the Hebrew verbs for "called" and "cried" are actually the same root in this verse, though Psalm 18 uses different words. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-22.html)

---

## vv. 8–10 — "Then the earth shook and quaked; the foundations of the heavens trembled; they were shaken because He burned with anger. Smoke rose from His nostrils, and consuming fire came from His mouth; glowing coals blazed forth. He parted the heavens and came down with dark clouds beneath His feet."

**Traditional reading:** This is theophanic language — God depicted as descending in judgment like He did at Mount Sinai (Exodus 19). Matthew Henry explains that the expressions are "borrowed from the descent of the divine Majesty upon Mount Sinai" but are used as "lofty metaphors" to set forth God's glory, displeasure against enemies, and readiness to help. Henry: "God's wisdom and power…which appeared in favour of David, were as clear and bright a discovery of God's glory to an eye of faith as such miraculous interpositions would have been to an eye of sense." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-samuel-22.html)

Boice: "What is most impressive…is the magnificent way the psalmist describes God rising from his throne in heaven in response to his servant's cry, parting the clouds, and descending to fight the king's battles accompanied by earthquakes, thunder, storms, and lightning." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/)

Ellicott notes that "foundations of the heavens" (2 Sam) differs from Psalm 18's "foundations of the hills" — the 2 Samuel text preserves the stronger poetic figure where mountains are "the pillars of heaven" (cf. Job 26:11). (https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/22.htm)

---

## vv. 11–13 — "He mounted a cherub and flew; He soared on the wings of the wind. He made darkness a canopy around Him, a gathering of water and thick clouds. From the brightness of His presence coals of fire blazed forth."

**Traditional reading:** David pictures God coming with glory and speed. Clarke says of the Hebrew: "The clap of the wing, the agitation and rush through the air are expressed here in a very extraordinary manner." The cherub is likely the storm-cloud chariot of God (cf. Ps 104:3; Ezek 1). The darkness canopy serves both for the amazement of enemies and the protection of God's people (Henry). Guzik: "David sees a God so loving that He won't tolerate the distress of His beloved." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-samuel-22.html)

**Anglican (Ellicott):** The 2 Samuel text reads "He was seen upon the wings of the wind," while Psalm 18 reads "he did fly." The two Hebrew words are exceedingly alike and either could be mistaken for the other; Psalm 18's reading is "far more poetical." (https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/22.htm)

---

## vv. 14–16 — "The LORD thundered from heaven; the voice of the Most High resounded. He shot His arrows and scattered the foes; He hurled lightning and routed them. The channels of the sea appeared, and the foundations of the world were exposed at the rebuke of the LORD, at the blast of the breath of His nostrils."

**Traditional reading:** The thunder is God's voice; the lightning is His arrows. Constable: "'Arrows' (v. 15) is a figure for lightning bolts." The "channels of the sea" and "foundations of the world exposed" evoke the parting of the Red Sea (Exodus 14–15). The Geneva Study Bible explicitly says: "He alludes to the miracle of the Red Sea." The Pulpit Commentary (citing Keil) clarifies that David's deliverance "was not actually attended by any such extraordinary natural phenomena; but the saving hand of God from heaven was so obviously manifested that the deliverance experienced by him could be poetically described as a miraculous interposition." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-22.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/2-samuel-22.html; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_samuel/22.htm)

**Reformed/Baptist (Piper):** Everything in creation — thunder, lightning, wind — serves to show that "the Lord was angry" on David's behalf. The thundering is His voice, the lightning is His arrows, the wind is His breath. The creation imagery is not about creation but about the Creator acting for His beloved. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/davids-god-entranced-song)

---

## vv. 17–18 — "He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters. He rescued me from my powerful enemy, from foes too mighty for me."

**Traditional reading:** Constable notes a parallel: "God had drawn David out of the waters of affliction as Pharaoh's daughter had drawn Moses out of literal dangerous waters." The "deep waters" (or "many waters") symbolize overwhelming trouble and chaos. David acknowledges that the enemy was genuinely too strong — "they were too strong for me" — making the deliverance entirely God's work. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-22.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/)

---

## vv. 19–20 — "They confronted me in my day of calamity, but the LORD was my support. He brought me out into the open; He rescued me because He delighted in me."

**Traditional reading:** Verse 20 is a high point. "He rescued me because He delighted in me" — David understood that his deliverance was rooted in relationship, not mere survival. Matthew Henry calls this "covenant-love" and sees David as "a type of Christ, whom God upheld because he delighted in him" (Isa 42:1). The "broad place" (or "open") signifies liberty, room to thrive, freedom from confinement. Guzik: "David had a sense of God's delight in him. His plea for deliverance was rooted in relationship, not merely in a desire to survive." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-samuel-22.html)

---

## vv. 21–25 — "The LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness; He has repaid me according to the cleanness of my hands. For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God. For all His ordinances are before me; I have not disregarded His statutes. And I have been blameless before Him and kept myself from iniquity. So the LORD has repaid me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness in His sight."

**This is the most debated passage in the chapter.** Here is what different traditions say:

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik, Enduring Word):** David is speaking as a forgiven man, not a sinless one. The text appears near the end of his life, after the sin with Bathsheba. "David knew he was a forgiven man, and that the cleanness of his hands was because God cleansed them, not because they had never been dirtied." Boice adds: "If we were to remind David of his sin with Bathsheba, he would claim it as an illustration and a proof of this principle since he suffered in a variety of ways as a consequence of that great sin." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/)

**Reformed Baptist (Piper, Desiring God):** This is not self-exaltation. "If he mentions his own righteousness, he measures it by the Lord's ways…It is from God that he has not wickedly departed." Piper summarises: "It is you who have made my way blameless — not sinless, but forgiven and faithful." David's righteousness is relative and derivative from God. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/davids-god-entranced-song)

**Baptist (Spurgeon, quoted in Precept Austin and Enduring Word):** "Before God the man after God's own heart was a humble sinner, but before his slanderers he could with unblushing face speak of the 'cleanness of his hands' and the righteousness of his life." David's claim is relative to his enemies' false accusations. On "I kept myself from my iniquity," Spurgeon quotes one who objected "Kept himself! Who made man his own keeper?" but acknowledges there is a sense in which believers must keep themselves from sin (cf. 2 Tim 2:21). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-22-commentary)

**Reformed (Geneva Study Bible):** Restricts the scope narrowly: David's righteousness is "toward Saul and my enemies" (v. 21 note), and "I attempted nothing without his commandment" (v. 22 note). The claim is limited to David's conduct in specific conflicts, not a claim of sinless perfection. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/2-samuel-22.html)

**Classic Evangelical (Matthew Henry):** David refers to his integrity regarding Saul, Ishbosheth, Absalom, and Sheba — those who "falsely accused him and misrepresented him." Henry is careful: "God had recompensed him, though not for his righteousness, as if that had merited any thing at the hand of God, yet according to his righteousness, which he was well pleased with, and had an eye to." Henry adds that David "kept himself from his own iniquity" — "he was afraid of sin and watchful against it." The matter of Uriah is "an exception (1 Kings 15:5), like that in Hezekiah's character, 2 Chronicles 32:31." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-samuel-22.html)

**Pulpit Commentary (broadly Protestant):** The language "neither implies entire freedom from sin nor indicates a boastful spirit, but is expressive of sincerity, integrity, fidelity; in contrast with the calumnies and wickedness of enemies." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_samuel/22.htm)

**Evangelical (Constable):** The psalmist is "not talking about justification by works, much less about sinless perfection, but about 'a conscience void of offence toward God and men' (Acts 24:16)." The Hebrew word for "cleanness" (*bor*) derives from washing hands with soda — a figure for moral purity. God "rewarded" David (not "saved" him) because of righteous conduct. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-22.html)

**Evangelical (Precept Austin / Today in the Word):** David's claim regarding his treatment of Saul is specifically true — he twice spared Saul's life. But "the more important reason for God's deliverance is God's own character." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2samuel_devotionals-2)

**Messianic reading (Gray's Concise Commentary):** Verses 20–28 "make it difficult to apply the psalm to David except in a highly poetical sense, and which gives it a Messianic significance" — pointing ultimately to the sinless Christ. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/2-samuel-22.html)

---

## v. 26 — "To the faithful You show Yourself faithful, to the blameless You show Yourself blameless."

**Traditional reading:** This is a principle of divine reciprocity that appears throughout Scripture. Guzik connects it to Jesus' words in Matthew 7:2: "with what judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you." Morgan: "God is to man what man is to God." David not only sang this principle but lived it — he showed mercy to Saul (1 Sam 24:10–13) and Shimei (2 Sam 16:7–12) and received mercy in return. Spurgeon adds: "Note that even the merciful need mercy; no amount of generosity to the poor, or forgiveness to enemies, can set us beyond the need of mercy." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-22/)

**Reformed Baptist (Piper):** This verse is part of David's argument that he is not exalting himself: "You are a merciful God…You lift up not the self-sufficient, but those who take refuge in you." The principle is ultimately about God's character, not a mechanical tit-for-tat. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/davids-god-entranced-song)

**Pulpit Commentary:** The same point is made as in the notes above on vv. 21–25 — the language expresses sincerity and integrity, not self-righteousness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-22.html)

---

## Summary of Where Protestant Traditions Differ

| Issue | Reformed/Baptist (Spurgeon, Piper, Boice) | Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik) | Classic Evangelical (Henry, Constable) |
|-------|-------------------------------------------|--------------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| David's righteousness claim (vv. 21–25) | Relative to enemies' slander; "not sinless, but forgiven and faithful" | David speaks as forgiven man; God cleansed his hands | Integrity regarding specific conflicts; Uriah is the exception |
| Theophany (vv. 8–16) | Poetic metaphor for real divine action | God moving all creation out of love for His beloved | Borrowed from Sinai; real glory manifested spiritually |
| "Kept myself from my iniquity" (v. 24) | A believer's responsibility, not self-salvation | David guarded against his besetting sin | Watchfulness against sin as evidence of integrity |
| Messianic element | Central (v. 51 climaxes in Christ; Piper develops fully) | Acknowledged but not the main emphasis | Present (Henry sees David as type of Christ in v. 20) |
